notes.b: Sedimentary rocks are built up in layers, and the boundaries between those layers decide how the rock later breaks and wears away. That is why landforms in layered rock start with strata and bedding planes.
points: Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers called strata, or beds, formed by deposition (sediment settling out) followed by compaction (squeezing together) and cementation (minerals gluing the grains).
A bedding plane is the boundary between one layer and the next; when the layers are laid down, bedding planes are roughly horizontal.
A bedding plane marks a pause or change in deposition, which is why neighbouring layers can differ.
Bedding planes divide the rock into layers, and each layer may differ in thickness and resistance (how well it stands up to erosion).
notes.tip: Bedding planes are horizontal, running parallel to the layers. Do not swap them with joints, which are vertical. Short-answer questions may ask you to define a bedding plane.

notes.b: Layers are cut by cracks as well as by planes between them. These cracks give water and ice a way into the rock.
points: A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place, so the rock on either side has not slid past.
Joints in sedimentary rock are at right angles to the bedding planes, so they are vertical (across the layers) where the strata are horizontal.
Joints form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock.
Bedding planes and joints together divide the rock into blocks.
notes.tip: Joints are vertical, across the layers; bedding planes are horizontal, along them. A sill is an igneous sheet that follows a bedding plane, so it is not a sedimentary structure. Expect a short definition question on joints.

notes.b: Earth movements can tilt layers that were laid down flat. The landform that results depends on how far and in which direction the strata tilt.
points: Dip is the angle at which strata tilt from the horizontal; the dip direction is the way they tilt.
Strike is the direction along a tilted layer's surface, at right angles to the dip.
Strata are horizontal, gently dipping or steeply dipping, and the landform depends on which, so you must state the attitude (tilt) of the layers when explaining a landform.
notes.tip: Here describe strata only as horizontal, gently dipping or steeply dipping. How they came to be tilted, folded or domed belongs to a later subsection.

notes.b: Bedding planes and joints are gaps in otherwise solid rock. Erosion does not attack the rock evenly but follows them.
points: Water, ice and weathering (the breakdown of rock in place) exploit bedding planes and joints as lines of weakness, because they can get into the rock there.
Rock breaks into blocks along these planes, so erosion is concentrated there.
notes.tip: Exams may ask how bedding planes and joints influence landform development. Say that they are lines of weakness, the rock breaks into blocks along them, and erosion concentrates there.

notes.b: Layers in a rock are not equally tough. Differential erosion means different layers wear away at different rates.
points: Where resistant layers, such as sandstone and limestone, alternate with weak layers, such as shale and clay, the weak layers are worn away faster.
The resistant layers are left standing out as cliffs and caps, because the soft rock around them has been removed.

notes.b: Rock layers also differ in whether water can pass through them. This controls where water sinks underground and where it comes back to the surface.
points: Water passes down joints and bedding planes in permeable (or pervious) rock, which lets water through.
Water flows over impermeable rock instead, because it cannot soak in.
A spring emerges where a permeable layer lies on an impermeable one, because the water sinking through the top layer is stopped by the layer below. The line of springs is a spring line.
notes.tip: No spring-line example is given for this subsection, so do not invent a named place.

notes.b: A plateau (a flat-topped upland) forms in layered rock. It needs horizontal strata with a tough layer on top.
points: 1. Horizontal strata have a resistant cap rock (the tough top layer) lying above weaker layers.
2. Erosion strips the weaker layers beneath the cap and wears back the edges of the upland, because weak rock wears away faster than the cap.
3. The cap protects the layers beneath, so the top stays flat and the edges stay steep.
Diagram: cross-section of a flat-topped upland with a resistant cap, cliffed edges and weaker strata below.

notes.b: When horizontal layers of hard and soft rock alternate several times, the plateau edge is not one cliff but a staircase.
points: Alternating hard and soft horizontal layers erode at different rates, because the hard rock resists erosion and the soft rock does not.
Hard layers form cliffs; soft layers form gentler slopes, often covered by scree (loose broken rock fragments), because the soft rock wears down more easily.
The profile of cliff and slope repeats for each pair of hard and soft layers.

notes.b: This is the Irish setting for landforms of horizontal strata. Near-horizontal Carboniferous strata (rocks laid down in the geological period of that name) of limestone, shale and sandstone form flat-topped uplands with steep cliffed edges and stepped slopes.
points: The Dartry Mountains and Cuilcagh span Co. Sligo, Co. Leitrim, Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
Caves and karst features (the landscape of limestone shaped by water) lie in the limestone beneath the uplands.
notes.tip: Benbulben and Cuilcagh have different cap rocks. Do not mix them.

notes.b: Benbulben, part of the Dartry Mountains, shows a resistant cap above weaker rock in one clear profile.
points: Benbulben, at 526 m, is a flat-topped mountain of near-horizontal strata.
A resistant limestone cap forms its vertical cliffs, because the cap resists erosion.
Weaker shale beneath forms the lower, gentler slopes, partly covered in scree.
Ice later steepened its sides.
notes.tip: Benbulben's cap is limestone. Cuilcagh's cap is sandstone.

notes.b: Cuilcagh has three rock types stacked on one another, so its profile is stepped rather than a single cliff.
points: Cuilcagh, at 665 m, is the highest point in both Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
A resistant sandstone cap lies over shale, which lies over limestone, giving a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge.
The Shannon Pot, the source of the River Shannon, lies at the foot of Cuilcagh in Co. Cavan.
The Marble Arch Caves, Co. Fermanagh, lie in the limestone beneath it.
notes.tip: Cuilcagh's cap is sandstone. Benbulben's cap is limestone.

notes.b: If erosion keeps working at a plateau, the plateau does not stay in one piece. It is cut into smaller flat-topped hills.
points: 1. Weathering and erosion work back the edges of a plateau.
2. The plateau is broken into separate flat-topped remnants (the parts left behind), each capped by the resistant rock.
3. A mesa is wider than it is high; a butte is a smaller, narrower remnant.
Example: Monument Valley, on the Arizona–Utah border, USA.
Diagram: cross-section of a mesa and a butte, each with a resistant cap.

notes.b: When strata tilt gently rather than lie flat, a resistant layer makes a ridge with one steep side and one gentle side. This ridge is an escarpment, or cuesta.
points: 1. On gently dipping strata, a resistant layer is exposed at the surface.
2. Erosion cuts a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers, because the cut ends of the resistant layer are exposed there.
3. The layers continue along the tilt as a long, gentle dip slope.
4. The weaker rock between cuestas is eroded into a vale (a low valley floor).
Example: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone cuesta with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east.
Diagram: cross-section of a cuesta showing scarp slope, dip slope and vale.
notes.tip: The scarp slope is steep and cuts across the layers; the dip slope is gentle and follows the layers. Short-answer questions may ask you to define escarpment and dip slope.

notes.b: If the strata dip steeply instead of gently, the same process gives a different shape.
points: A hogback forms on steeply dipping strata.
It is a narrow ridge whose scarp and dip slopes are of nearly equal steepness, unlike a cuesta, where one slope is steep and the other gentle.
Example: the Hog's Back, Surrey, England, a narrow chalk ridge.

notes.h: Bedding planes and joints in smaller landforms
notes.b: Bedding planes and joints also shape smaller features. These are named here as effects of the structures; how each forms is taught elsewhere.
points: Joints and bedding planes in limestone give limestone pavement, with blocks called clints separated by grikes (the gaps between them).
Caves form along bedding planes in limestone.
Waterfalls form over horizontal cap rock.
Sea caves and arches form along joints on the coast.

notes.b: The Paris Basin is the international example of gently dipping strata. It is a saucer-shaped basin of sedimentary layers of different resistance, dipping gently in towards Paris.
points: The layers are limestone, chalk and clay.
Paris lies near the centre of the basin.
On the eastern side, resistant layers form outward-facing escarpments (cuestas), with dip slopes facing in towards Paris.
Clay vales lie between the escarpments, because the weaker clay is worn away faster.

notes.b: The Brecon Beacons are a second international example of gently dipping strata, this time in sandstone.
points: Gently dipping Old Red Sandstone forms flat-topped summits.
The summits have steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes.
Pen y Fan, at 886 m, is the highest peak in southern Britain.
The area was renamed Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in 2023.
notes.tip: The syllabus gives the Paris Basin and the Brecon Beacons as international settings, so be ready to link the dip of the strata to the shape of the slopes.

keyTerms.definition: Layers of sedimentary rock, laid down by deposition and then compacted and cemented.
The boundary between one sedimentary layer and the next, roughly horizontal when the layers are laid down.
A crack in rock along which no movement has taken place, here at right angles to the bedding planes in sedimentary rock.
The angle at which strata tilt from the horizontal.
The direction along a tilted layer's surface, at right angles to the dip.
A bedding plane or joint along which water, ice and weathering break the rock.
Rock through which water can pass, down joints and bedding planes.
A line of springs where a permeable layer lies on an impermeable one.
The steep slope cut across the edges of tilted layers.
The gentle slope that follows the tilt of the layers.
An asymmetric ridge on gently dipping strata, with a steep scarp slope and a long dip slope.
A flat-topped hill with a resistant cap, wider than it is high.
A smaller, narrower flat-topped remnant with a resistant cap.
A narrow ridge on steeply dipping strata, with scarp and dip slopes of nearly equal steepness.
The blocks of limestone pavement (clints) separated by the cracks between them (grikes).

factCards.term: Joints in sedimentary rock: how they form and what they do
factCards.definition: They form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock. They run at right angles to the bedding planes, so together the two divide the rock into blocks.

factCards.term: How bedding planes and joints guide erosion of layered rock
factCards.definition: Water, ice and weathering exploit bedding planes and joints, so rock breaks into blocks and erosion is concentrated there. Where resistant sandstone or limestone alternates with weak shale or clay, the weak layers wear faster, leaving cliffs and caps.

factCards.term: Plateau on horizontal strata: formation in three stages
factCards.definition: First, a resistant cap rock lies above weaker horizontal layers; then erosion strips the weaker layers beneath the cap and wears back the edges; finally, the cap protects the layers beneath, so the top stays flat and the edges stay steep.

factCards.term: Stepped slopes: how alternating layers produce them
factCards.definition: Hard and soft horizontal layers erode at different rates: hard layers form cliffs and soft layers form gentler slopes, often covered by scree, so the cliff-and-slope profile repeats for each pair of layers.

Benbulben, Co. Sligo (526 m), in the Dartry Mountains: near-horizontal strata with a resistant limestone cap forming vertical cliffs over weaker shale, which forms gentler lower slopes partly covered in scree. Ice later steepened its sides.

factCards.term: Cuilcagh: height, structure and features at its foot
factCards.definition: At 665 m it is the highest point in Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh: a resistant sandstone cap over shale over limestone gives a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge. The Shannon Pot lies at its foot and the Marble Arch Caves in the limestone beneath.

factCards.term: Mesa and butte: formation and a named example
factCards.definition: Weathering and erosion work back the edges of a plateau, breaking it into flat-topped remnants capped by resistant rock: a mesa is wider than it is high; a butte is a smaller, narrower remnant. Example: Monument Valley, on the Arizona–Utah border, USA.

First, a resistant layer is exposed on gently dipping strata; then erosion cuts a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers; the layer continues along the tilt as a long, gentle dip slope; finally the weaker rock between cuestas is eroded into a vale.

factCards.term: Name an example of a cuesta and of a hogback
factCards.definition: Cuesta: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone ridge with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east. Hogback: the Hog's Back, Surrey, England, a narrow chalk ridge on steeply dipping strata.

A saucer-shaped basin of limestone, chalk and clay layers dipping gently in towards Paris, near its centre. On the eastern side resistant layers form escarpments facing outwards (east), with dip slopes facing in towards Paris and clay vales between them.

factCards.term: Brecon Beacons: rock, landforms and highest peak
factCards.definition: Gently dipping Old Red Sandstone forms flat-topped summits with steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes. Pen y Fan (886 m) is the highest peak in southern Britain. The area was renamed Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in 2023.

factCards.term: Bedding planes and joints: four smaller landforms they produce
factCards.definition: Limestone pavement, with clints separated by grikes; caves along bedding planes in limestone; waterfalls over horizontal cap rock; sea caves and arches along joints on the coast.

questions.prompt: Examine how sedimentary structures influence the development of landforms, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Bedding planes and joints are lines of weakness: water, ice and weathering exploit them, so rock breaks into blocks along them and erosion is concentrated there. Where resistant layers alternate with weak layers, the weak layers are worn away faster and the resistant layers stand out as cliffs and caps, a process of differential erosion. Where strata are horizontal, a resistant cap protects the layers beneath and the result is a plateau with a flat top and steep edges. Benbulben, Co. Sligo, at 526 m, is a flat-topped mountain of near-horizontal strata: a limestone cap forms vertical cliffs, and weaker shale beneath forms gentler slopes partly covered in scree. Cuilcagh, at 665 m, has a sandstone cap over shale over limestone, giving a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge. Monument Valley, USA, shows how the edges of a plateau retreat into mesas and buttes. Permeability controls water: water passes down joints and bedding planes in permeable rock and flows over impermeable rock, and springs emerge where permeable rock lies on impermeable rock. Where strata dip gently, the Paris Basin shows the result: resistant limestone and chalk form outward-facing cuestas with steep scarp slopes and gentle dip slopes, and clay vales lie between them. The Brecon Beacons in south Wales have gently dipping Old Red Sandstone, with steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes. Limestone areas also carry karst features, such as clints and grikes on pavements and caves along bedding planes.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, how an escarpment (cuesta) forms.
questions.model: A cuesta forms on gently dipping strata where a resistant layer lies over weaker layers. Diagram: a labelled cross-section showing the dipping resistant layer, the weaker layer beneath it, the steep scarp slope, the long gentle dip slope following the tilt of the resistant layer, and the vale eroded in the weaker rock. Stage 1: the strata are tilted gently, so a resistant layer such as limestone or chalk lies over softer clay or shale. Stage 2: erosion removes the weaker rock beneath the resistant layer at the edge, cutting a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers. Stage 3: the resistant layer continues along its tilt, forming a long, gentle dip slope on the other side. Stage 4: the weaker rock between two cuestas is eroded into a clay vale. Example: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone cuesta with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east. The Paris Basin has a series of cuestas with escarpments facing outwards and dip slopes facing in towards Paris.

questions.prompt: Explain the terms bedding plane and joint.
questions.model: A bedding plane is the boundary between one sedimentary layer and the next, roughly horizontal when the layers are laid down; it marks a pause or change in deposition. A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place; in sedimentary rock joints are at right angles to the bedding planes and form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock.
